cards.q: Define lattice enthalpy of formation (Edexcel: lattice energy).
cards.a: The enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions, under standard conditions.
cards.why: It is always exothermic (negative), because the oppositely charged ions attract each other.

cards.q: Define lattice enthalpy of dissociation, and say how it relates to lattice enthalpy of formation.
cards.a: The enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid is separated into its gaseous ions. It has the same size as the lattice enthalpy of formation but the opposite sign.
cards.why: Dissociation breaks the attractions between ions, so it is always endothermic (positive).

cards.q: Write the equation for the lattice enthalpy of formation of sodium chloride.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Na^{+}(g) + Cl^{-}(g) \rightarrow NaCl(s)}\)
cards.why: Gaseous ions on the left, one mole of solid on the right. The dissociation equation is the reverse.

cards.q: Define standard enthalpy of atomisation, \(\Delta_{\text{at}}H^{\circ}\).
cards.a: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state, under standard conditions.
cards.why: It is always endothermic: bonds or metallic bonding must be broken.

cards.q: Write equations for the enthalpy of atomisation of sodium and of chlorine.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Na(s) \rightarrow Na(g)}\)
\(\mathrm{\tfrac{1}{2}Cl_{2}(g) \rightarrow Cl(g)}\)
cards.why: One mole of gaseous atoms is formed each time, so only half a mole of chlorine molecules is needed.

cards.q: The Cl–Cl bond enthalpy is \(+243\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). What is the enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine?
cards.a: \(+121.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) (half the bond enthalpy).
cards.why: Bond enthalpy breaks one mole of \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\), giving two moles of Cl atoms; atomisation makes only one mole of Cl atoms.

cards.q: Define first electron affinity.
cards.a: The enthalpy change when each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms gains one electron to form one mole of gaseous 1− ions.
cards.why: For chlorine: \(\mathrm{Cl(g) + e^{-} \rightarrow Cl^{-}(g)}\), \(-349\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

cards.q: Explain why the first electron affinity of oxygen is exothermic but the second is endothermic.
cards.a: The first electron is attracted to the nucleus; the second is repelled by the negative ion.
marks: First: the incoming electron is attracted by the nucleus, so energy is released.
Second: the electron is added to an \(\mathrm{O^{-}}\) ion, which is already negative.
Energy must be supplied to overcome the repulsion between the ion and the electron, so it is endothermic.

cards.q: Write the equation for the second electron affinity of oxygen.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{O^{-}(g) + e^{-} \rightarrow O^{2-}(g)}\)
cards.why: Every species is gaseous, and one electron is added to the 1− ion.

cards.q: Define first ionisation energy, as used in a Born–Haber cycle, and write the equation for sodium.
cards.a:
The enthalpy change to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
\(\mathrm{Na(g) \rightarrow Na^{+}(g) + e^{-}}\)
cards.why: Ionisation energies are always endothermic.

cards.q: List the steps of the Born–Haber cycle for sodium chloride, going from the elements to the gaseous ions.
cards.a: Atomise sodium, then ionise it (\(\mathrm{Na(g) \rightarrow Na^{+}(g)}\)); atomise chlorine, then add an electron (first electron affinity).
cards.why: The lattice enthalpy then joins the gaseous ions to the solid, and the enthalpy of formation joins the elements directly to the solid.

cards.q: Calculate the lattice energy (enthalpy of lattice formation) of NaCl. Data in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H\) NaCl \(-411\); \(\Delta_{\text{at}}H\) Na \(+107\); first IE Na \(+496\); \(\Delta_{\text{at}}H\) Cl \(+122\); first EA Cl \(-349\).
cards.a: \(-787\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Both routes from the elements to the solid have the same total enthalpy change.

cards.q: Calculate the lattice energy (enthalpy of lattice formation) of \(\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}\). Data in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H\) \(-641\); \(\Delta_{\text{at}}H\) Mg \(+148\); IE Mg: first \(+738\), second \(+1451\); \(\Delta_{\text{at}}H\) Cl \(+122\); first EA Cl \(-349\).
cards.a: \(-2524\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
steps: Two Cl atoms and two electron affinities are needed: \(2(122) = 244\) and \(2(-349) = -698\).
cards.why: Multiply the chlorine steps by two, and include both ionisation energies of magnesium.

cards.q: Calculate the lattice energy (enthalpy of lattice formation) of MgO. Data in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H\) \(-602\); \(\Delta_{\text{at}}H\) Mg \(+148\); IE Mg: first \(+738\), second \(+1451\); \(\Delta_{\text{at}}H\) O \(+249\); EA O: first \(-141\), second \(+798\).
cards.a: \(-3845\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: The second electron affinity of oxygen is positive: watch the sign.

cards.q: Use a Born–Haber cycle to find the first electron affinity of chlorine. Data in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H\) KCl \(-437\); lattice energy KCl \(-718\); \(\Delta_{\text{at}}H\) K \(+89\); first IE K \(+419\); \(\Delta_{\text{at}}H\) Cl \(+122\).
cards.a: \(-349\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Any one quantity in the cycle can be found if all the others are known.

cards.q: Explain why the lattice energy of MgO is much more exothermic than that of NaCl.
cards.a: The ions in MgO have higher charges and smaller radii, so they attract each other more strongly.
marks: \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) have twice the charges of \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\).
The ions in MgO are smaller, so they are closer together.
So the electrostatic attraction between ions is stronger, and more energy is released when the lattice forms.

cards.q: Put NaF, NaCl and NaBr in order of increasingly exothermic lattice energy, and explain.
cards.a: NaBr < NaCl < NaF (most exothermic).
cards.why: The charges are the same, but the anion gets smaller from \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\) to \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\), so the ions are closer and attract more strongly. Lattice energy measures ionic bond strength.

cards.q: What does the perfect ionic model assume when lattice energy is calculated from electrostatic theory?
cards.a: The ions are perfect spheres with their charge evenly spread (point charges), and the only interaction is electrostatic attraction and repulsion between ions.
cards.why: This value is called the theoretical lattice energy; the Born–Haber value is the experimental one.

cards.q: The experimental (Born–Haber) lattice energy of silver iodide is considerably more exothermic than the theoretical value. Explain what this shows.
cards.a: Silver iodide has a significant degree of covalent bonding.
marks: The theoretical value assumes a perfectly ionic compound of spherical ions.
In AgI the cation distorts (polarises) the large iodide ion, drawing electron density between the ions.
This partial sharing of electrons adds covalent character, which makes the bonding stronger than the ionic model predicts.
The bigger the difference between the two values, the greater the covalent character.

cards.q: For sodium chloride the Born–Haber and theoretical lattice energies agree closely. What does this tell you?
cards.a: Sodium chloride is almost perfectly ionic: the ionic model describes its bonding well.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) has only a 1+ charge and is fairly large, so it hardly distorts the \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ion.

cards.q: What is meant by polarisation, as applied to ions?
cards.a: The distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a neighbouring cation, which attracts electron density towards itself.
cards.why: If the distortion is large, electron density builds up between the ions and the bond gains covalent character.

cards.q: What makes a cation strongly polarising?
cards.a: A small radius and a high charge: a high charge density.
marks: A higher charge attracts the anion’s electrons more strongly.
A smaller cation concentrates its charge, so it can approach the anion closely and has a stronger effect.
So \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) is more polarising than \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\), which is more polarising than \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\).

cards.q: What makes an anion easily polarised?
cards.a: A large radius and a high charge.
marks: In a large anion the outer electrons are far from the nucleus and well shielded, so they are held weakly and easily distorted.
A higher negative charge means more electrons for the nucleus to hold, so the cloud is distorted more easily.
So \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\) is more polarisable than \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\).

cards.q: Which has the greater covalent character: lithium iodide or potassium fluoride? Explain.
cards.a: Lithium iodide.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{Li^{+}}\) is very small, so it is strongly polarising, and \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\) is large, so it is easily polarised. \(\mathrm{K^{+}}\) is large and \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\) small, so KF is nearly perfectly ionic.

cards.q: Define enthalpy change of hydration, \(\Delta_{\text{hyd}}H\).
cards.a: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water to form one mole of aqueous ions.
cards.why: For example \(\mathrm{Na^{+}(g) + aq \rightarrow Na^{+}(aq)}\). It is always exothermic, because water molecules are attracted to the ion.

cards.q: Define enthalpy change of solution, \(\Delta_{\text{sol}}H\).
cards.a: The enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid dissolves in enough water to form a solution in which the ions are far enough apart not to interact.
cards.why: For example \(\mathrm{NaCl(s) + aq \rightarrow Na^{+}(aq) + Cl^{-}(aq)}\). It can be exothermic or endothermic.

cards.q: How is the enthalpy of solution related to the lattice enthalpy and the enthalpies of hydration?
cards.a: \(\Delta_{\text{sol}}H = \Delta H_{\text{lattice dissociation}} + \sum \Delta_{\text{hyd}}H\)
cards.why: The solid is first broken into gaseous ions (endothermic), which are then hydrated (exothermic). With a lattice energy of formation, subtract it instead of adding.

cards.q: Calculate \(\Delta_{\text{sol}}H\) of NaCl. Data in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): lattice energy (formation) \(-787\); \(\Delta_{\text{hyd}}H\): \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) \(-406\), \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) \(-378\).
cards.a: \(+3\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
steps: Breaking the lattice into gaseous ions: \(+787\)
cards.why: A small positive value: salt dissolves with only a slight cooling.

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{MgCl_{2}}\): lattice dissociation enthalpy \(+2526\), \(\Delta_{\text{sol}}H\) \(-155\), \(\Delta_{\text{hyd}}H( \mathrm{Cl^{-}})\) \(-378\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Calculate \(\Delta_{\text{hyd}}H( \mathrm{Mg^{2+}})\).
cards.a: \(-1925\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: There are two chloride ions per formula unit, so the chloride hydration enthalpy is doubled.

cards.q: Explain why the enthalpy of hydration of \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) is much more exothermic than that of \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\).
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) has a higher charge and a smaller radius.
marks: Water molecules are attracted to a cation by their \(\delta-\) oxygen atoms.
\(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) has a greater charge and is smaller, so it has a higher charge density.
The attraction to the water molecules is stronger, so more energy is released.

cards.q: How are water molecules arranged around a hydrated cation and a hydrated anion?
cards.a: Around a cation, the \(\delta-\) oxygen atoms point towards the ion. Around an anion, the \(\delta+\) hydrogen atoms point towards the ion.
cards.why: Each ion is surrounded by water molecules held by these electrostatic attractions.

cards.q: On an energy level diagram for dissolving an ionic solid, what must be true for the enthalpy of solution to be endothermic?
cards.a: The energy needed to break the lattice into gaseous ions must be greater than the energy released when those ions are hydrated.
cards.why: The gaseous ions are drawn at the top; the hydrated ions finish above the solid if dissolving is endothermic.

cards.q: Why can enthalpy change alone not decide whether a reaction happens?
cards.a: Some endothermic reactions and processes happen on their own at room temperature, such as dissolving ammonium nitrate in water.
cards.why: The entropy change must also be considered.

cards.q: What is entropy, \(S\), and what are its units?
cards.a: A measure of the disorder of a system: the number of ways the particles and their energy can be arranged. Units: \(\text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
cards.why: The natural direction of change is towards increasing total entropy.

cards.q: How does entropy change on melting and on boiling?
cards.a: It increases each time: \(S\)(solid) < \(S\)(liquid) < \(S\)(gas). The increase on boiling is much larger.
cards.why: Gas particles move freely and randomly, with far more possible arrangements than in a liquid or solid.

cards.q: Predict the sign of \(\Delta S\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2NH_{3}(g)}\) and explain.
cards.a: Negative. Four moles of gas become two moles of gas.
cards.why: Fewer gas particles means fewer ways of arranging them, so the system becomes more ordered.

cards.q: Why does the entropy of the system usually increase when an ionic solid dissolves in water?
cards.a: Ions held in fixed positions in an ordered lattice become free to move randomly through the solution.
cards.why: This is why some endothermic salts, such as ammonium nitrate, still dissolve readily.

cards.q: Solid barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)₂·8H₂O, and solid ammonium chloride react when mixed, and the flask gets cold enough to freeze water on its outside. Why is this endothermic reaction feasible?
cards.a: Two solids produce ammonia gas, liquid water and a solution: a large increase in the entropy of the system.
cards.why: \(\Delta S_{\text{system}}\) is large and positive, so it outweighs the negative \(\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}\) caused by taking in heat.

cards.q: Ethanoic acid reacts with ammonium carbonate. The mixture cools, yet the reaction happens readily. Explain in terms of entropy.
cards.a: Carbon dioxide gas is produced: \(\mathrm{2CH_{3}COOH + (NH_{4})_{2}CO_{3} \rightarrow 2CH_{3}COONH_{4} + H_{2}O + CO_{2}}\).
cards.why: Forming a gas from a solid and a solution increases the disorder, so \(\Delta S_{\text{system}}\) is positive and large enough to make \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) positive.

cards.q: Burning magnesium, \(\mathrm{2Mg(s) + O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2MgO(s)}\), decreases the entropy of the system. Why does it still happen?
cards.a: It is very exothermic, so it releases a lot of heat to the surroundings, making \(\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}\) large and positive.
cards.why: \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) is positive even though \(\Delta S_{\text{system}}\) is negative (a gas is used up).

cards.q: Calculate \(\Delta S\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2NH_{3}(g)}\). \(S\) in \(\text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\): \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\) 192, \(\mathrm{H_{2}}\) 131, \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) 193.
cards.a: \(-199\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: The negative sign fits the drop from four moles of gas to two.

cards.q: Calculate \(\Delta S\) for \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s) \rightarrow CaO(s) + CO_{2}(g)}\). \(S\) in \(\text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\): \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}\) 93, \(\mathrm{CaO}\) 40, \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) 214.
cards.a: \(+161\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: A gas is formed from a solid, so the entropy increases.

cards.q: True or false: like \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H^{\circ}\), the standard entropy of an element such as \(\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\) is zero.
cards.a: False. Elements have positive standard entropies; \(S\) of \(\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\) is about \(205\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
cards.why: Entropies are absolute values, not changes, so every substance above 0 K has a positive entropy. Include the elements in the calculation.

cards.q: Give the equations for \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) and \(\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}\).
cards.a:
\(\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_{\text{system}} + \Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}\)
\(\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} = -\frac{\Delta H}{T}\)
cards.why: A reaction is feasible when \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) is positive. Convert \(\Delta H\) to J so that the units match.

cards.q: Why is \(\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} = -\frac{\Delta H}{T}\) larger at low temperatures?
cards.a: Releasing a given amount of heat into cold surroundings increases their disorder more than releasing it into hot surroundings, which are already very disordered.
cards.why: An exothermic reaction (\(\Delta H\) negative) makes \(\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}\) positive.

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2NH_{3}(g)}\), \(\Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S_{\text{system}} = -199\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). Calculate \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) at 298 K.
cards.a: \(+110\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\): feasible.
cards.why: \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) is positive, so the reaction is feasible at 298 K.

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{2Mg(s) + O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2MgO(s)}\), \(\Delta H = -1202\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). \(S\) in \(\text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\): Mg 32.7, \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) 205.0, MgO 26.9. Calculate \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) at 298 K.
cards.a: \(+3820\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: The huge positive entropy change of the surroundings outweighs the decrease in the system.

cards.q: Give the Gibbs free-energy equation and the condition for a reaction to be feasible.
cards.a:
\(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\)
Feasible when \(\Delta G \le 0\).
cards.why: \(\Delta G\) is in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), so \(\Delta S\) must be converted from \(\text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) to \(\text{kJ K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) (divide by 1000). Edexcel writes \(\Delta S_{\text{system}}\).

cards.q: Show how \(\Delta G\) is related to \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\).
cards.a: \(\Delta G = -T\Delta S_{\text{total}}\), so a positive \(\Delta S_{\text{total}}\) means a negative \(\Delta G\).
cards.why: Multiply \(\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_{\text{system}} - \frac{\Delta H}{T}\) by \(-T\): \(-T\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta H - T\Delta S_{\text{system}} = \Delta G\).

cards.q: How do the signs of \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta S\) decide when a reaction is feasible?
cards.a:
\(\Delta H\) −, \(\Delta S\) +: feasible at all temperatures.
\(\Delta H\) +, \(\Delta S\) −: never feasible.
\(\Delta H\) −, \(\Delta S\) −: feasible at low temperatures.
\(\Delta H\) +, \(\Delta S\) +: feasible at high temperatures.
cards.why: When the signs are the same, the \(T\Delta S\) term decides, and its size grows with temperature.

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{CaCO_{3}(s) \rightarrow CaO(s) + CO_{2}(g)}\), \(\Delta H = +178\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S = +161\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). Calculate \(\Delta G\) at 298 K. Is the reaction feasible?
cards.a: \(+130\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): not feasible at 298 K.
cards.why: \(\Delta G\) is positive, which is why limestone does not decompose at room temperature.

cards.q: Using \(\Delta H = +178\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S = +161\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\), find the minimum temperature at which calcium carbonate decomposition becomes feasible.
cards.a: \(1110\ \text{K}\)
steps: The reaction just becomes feasible when \(\Delta G = 0\), so \(T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}\).
cards.why: Above this temperature the TΔS term outweighs ΔH. Lime kilns are run above this temperature.

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow H_{2}O(g)}\), \(\Delta H = +40.7\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S = +109\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). Calculate the temperature at which water boils at 100 kPa.
cards.a: \(373\ \text{K}\)
steps: At the boiling point liquid and gas are in equilibrium, so \(\Delta G = 0\).
cards.why: \(373\ \text{K}\) is \(100\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), the normal boiling point of water.

cards.q: Ethanol boils at \(351\ \text{K}\), and its enthalpy of vaporisation is \(+38.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Calculate its entropy of vaporisation.
cards.a: \(+110\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)
steps: At the boiling point \(\Delta G = 0\), so \(\Delta S = \frac{\Delta H}{T}\).
cards.why: Use ΔH in J to get ΔS in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

cards.q: A graph of \(\Delta G\) (in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)) against \(T\) is a straight line through \((200, +50)\) and \((400, +10)\). Find \(\Delta S\), \(\Delta H\), and the temperature at which the reaction becomes feasible.
cards.a: \(\Delta S = +200\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\), \(\Delta H = +90\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), feasible above \(450\ \text{K}\).
steps: Gradient \(= \frac{10 - 50}{400 - 200} = -0.20\ \text{kJ K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). Since \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\), gradient \(= -\Delta S\), so \(\Delta S = +0.20\ \text{kJ K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
The intercept at \(T = 0\) is \(\Delta H\): \(50 = \Delta H - 200 \times 0.20\), so \(\Delta H = +90\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).
cards.why: On a \(\Delta G\)–\(T\) graph, the gradient is \(-\Delta S\) and the intercept on the \(\Delta G\) axis is \(\Delta H\).

cards.q: A graph of \(\Delta G\) against \(T\) for a reaction suddenly changes gradient at one temperature. Why?
cards.a: A reactant or product changes state at that temperature (for example, water boils), which changes \(\Delta S\) for the reaction.
cards.why: The gradient of the line is \(-\Delta S\), so a new \(\Delta S\) gives a new gradient.

cards.q: Explain, using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, why ice melts above 273 K but not below.
cards.a: Melting is endothermic with a positive entropy change, so it becomes feasible only when TΔS is larger than ΔH.
marks: Melting has ΔH positive (energy is needed to break some hydrogen bonds) and ΔS positive (the liquid is more disordered).
Below 273 K, TΔS is smaller than ΔH, so ΔG is positive and melting is not feasible.
Above 273 K, TΔS is larger than ΔH, so ΔG is negative and melting is feasible; at 273 K, ΔG = 0.

cards.q: True or false: in \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) you can use \(\Delta H\) in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta S\) in \(\text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) as given in data tables.
cards.a: False. Convert \(\Delta S\) to \(\text{kJ K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) (divide by 1000) first.
cards.why: Otherwise the \(T\Delta S\) term is 1000 times too large and the feasibility conclusion may be wrong.

cards.q: True or false: all exothermic reactions are feasible.
cards.a: False. If \(\Delta S\) is negative, an exothermic reaction becomes not feasible above \(T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}\).
cards.why: At high temperature the \(-T\Delta S\) term becomes positive and large enough to make \(\Delta G\) positive.

cards.q: Give the equation linking \(\Delta G\) to the equilibrium constant, \(K\), and what it shows.
cards.a: \(\Delta G = -RT\ln K\)
cards.why: A negative \(\Delta G\) gives \(\ln K > 0\), so \(K > 1\): feasible reactions have large equilibrium constants, with products favoured. \(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).

cards.q: A reaction has \(\Delta G = -20.0\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) at 298 K. Calculate \(K\). (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(K = 3.2 \times 10^{3}\)
cards.why: Use \(\Delta G\) in J, to match the units of \(R\).

cards.q: An equilibrium has \(K = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}\) at 298 K. Calculate \(\Delta G\). (\(R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(+28.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: A small \(K\) (reactants favoured) goes with a positive \(\Delta G\): not feasible.

cards.q: Explain why a reaction with a negative \(\Delta G\) may not take place in practice.
cards.a: It may have a very high activation energy, so the rate is negligibly slow: it is kinetically inert.
marks: A negative \(\Delta G\) shows only that the reaction is thermodynamically feasible.
\(\Delta G\) says nothing about rate; if the activation energy is high, very few collisions have enough energy to react.
For example, methane and oxygen do not react until a spark is applied.
Also, \(\Delta G^{\circ}\) values apply to standard conditions, which may differ from the actual conditions.

cards.q: Diamond turning into graphite has a negative \(\Delta G\) at room temperature. Why do diamonds last?
cards.a: The change is kinetically inhibited: the activation energy is so high that the rate at room temperature is effectively zero.
cards.why: Thermodynamically feasible reactions can be prevented by kinetic factors.

cards.q: True or false: a feasible reaction will happen quickly.
cards.a: False. Feasibility says whether a reaction can happen, not how fast.
cards.why: The rate depends on the activation energy, which \(\Delta G\) does not tell you.
